paragraphs: Detecting three-dimensional objects from a single image requires training examples with varied objects and reliable spatial labels. This paper increases that variety by inserting virtual objects into photographs of real indoor scenes. Its central concern is making the additions physically plausible within cluttered rooms, so the augmented images provide useful training examples.

The method first finds feasible positions and orientations for each inserted object, avoiding collisions with the existing room layout. It then estimates illumination at the chosen location. Accounting for lighting that varies across space helps the rendered object match its surroundings, including its appearance and cast shadows. The inserted objects also come with three-dimensional bounding boxes.

The authors report significant improvements to existing monocular 3D detection models and state-of-the-art performance using this augmentation. The finding connects the quality of generated training content to a downstream recognition task: plausible placement and rendering can make synthetic additions useful for learning from real scenes. The demonstrated application concerns complex indoor scenes and detection from individual images.
neurips-2023-3d-copy-paste-physically-pl.tldr: Physically plausible virtual objects inserted into real indoor scenes improve training for monocular 3D object detection.

paragraphs: Text-attributed graphs combine two sources of information: descriptions attached to individual nodes and connections between those nodes. Learning useful representations requires integrating what the text says with how the graph is organized. The paper addresses a practical obstacle to studying this integration: a shortage of meaningful datasets and standardized evaluation procedures.

The authors introduce CS-TAG, a collection of large, challenging datasets covering multiple domains, including citation networks and purchase graphs. This breadth provides a shared setting for examining approaches across different kinds of textual and structural information. Standardized procedures accompany the datasets, making evaluation a central part of the contribution.

The study benchmarks pretrained language models, graph neural networks, and methods that train the two together. It also proposes topological pretraining of language models, bringing graph structure into language-model pretraining. The contribution is a benchmark collection, evaluation framework, and set of baseline experiments for investigating these learning choices. The abstract establishes this comparative foundation without declaring a single learning paradigm the overall winner.
neurips-2023-a-comprehensive-study-on-te.tldr: CS-TAG provides large, diverse text-attributed graph datasets and standardized experiments for studying how language and graph models interact.

paragraphs: One explanation for adversarial vulnerability is that adversarial examples contain non-robust features that still help predict labels. Their usefulness under supervised learning has supported the idea that these features carry meaningful predictive information, even when they resemble noise to people. This paper asks how far that usefulness extends across different ways of learning.

The authors examine non-robust features in contrastive learning, masked image modeling, and diffusion models. They find that features useful for supervised classification transfer poorly to these self-supervised paradigms. Robust and natural features show better transferability across the examined paradigms. This comparison broadens the test of usefulness beyond success in one training setup.

The paper also examines whether robust features are enough to produce robust models. Encoders trained naturally from those features remain largely vulnerable under AutoAttack. Together, the findings suggest that non-robust features may function as shortcuts specific to a learning paradigm, while robust features alone might not deliver reliable robustness. These are conclusions from the cross-paradigm examination, rather than a universal proof that adversarial features carry no information.
neurips-2023-adversarial-examples-are-no.tldr: Cross-paradigm experiments suggest non-robust features behave like learning-specific shortcuts, while robust features alone may not ensure model robustness.

paragraphs: Network intrusion detectors need to learn about new threats while retaining knowledge of older ones. Memory replay supports this continual learning by revisiting stored examples. The paper targets two difficulties in making replay effective at scale: severe imbalance between classes and the computational expense of choosing examples whose knowledge is most threatened by new updates.

The first contribution extends class balancing reservoir sampling to handle severe class imbalance in large datasets. The second, PAPA, uses a Gaussian mixture model to approximate parameter behavior when identifying maximally interfering samples. Its purpose is to reduce the virtual stochastic gradient updates required during sample selection, lowering the cost of deciding what to replay.

The authors report substantial improvements over baselines on intrusion detection benchmarks spanning shorter collection periods and a longer period with distribution shift. They also validate the approaches on continual learning and anomaly detection benchmarks. PAPA reduces training time by 12–40% relative to the maximally interfered samples retrieval algorithm. These results address both detection performance and the overhead of maintaining useful replay.
neurips-2023-augmented-memory-replay-bas.tldr: Improved replay balancing and cheaper interference estimation strengthen continual intrusion detection while reducing replay-related training costs.

paragraphs: With a fixed sampling budget, best-arm identification asks which uncertain option has the highest expected reward. The challenge is distributing observations so that the final choice is unlikely to be wrong. Error rates are easier to analyze when the sampling plan is fixed in advance; adaptive sampling makes that analysis substantially harder.

The paper connects large-deviation behavior of the observed sampling proportions to that of the observed arm rewards. Large-deviation analysis describes how probabilities of unusual outcomes shrink as more samples are collected. The connection applies to any adaptive algorithm and gives the authors a way to sharpen error upper bounds for existing methods, including Successive Rejects.

The same framework motivates Continuous Rejects, which can eliminate an arm in any round using observed reward gaps. This gives the algorithm flexibility to react as evidence accumulates. The authors prove stronger performance guarantees than those of existing algorithms, including Successive Rejects, and report supporting numerical experiments. The work advances adaptive error analysis without claiming to fully characterize the minimum instance-specific error probability.
neurips-2023-best-arm-identification-wit.tldr: A large-deviation framework sharpens adaptive best-arm error guarantees and supports Continuous Rejects, an algorithm that can eliminate arms at any round.

paragraphs: Mutual information measures statistical dependence and is used in fields ranging from representation learning to computational biology. Estimating it from data can be difficult, yet estimators are often tested on relatively narrow distribution families. The paper argues for broader evaluation than multivariate normal distributions and selected cases involving one-dimensional variables.

The authors construct a diverse family of distributions whose true mutual information is known. Having a known answer makes it possible to assess estimation quality directly across more varied settings. They also introduce a benchmarking platform that is independent of programming language, providing a common basis for evaluating different implementations and approaches.

The study considers both classical and neural estimators under high dimensionality, sparse interactions, long tails, and high mutual information. It discusses where these methods apply and where they encounter difficulties, then offers guidance for selecting an estimator and approaching a new dataset. Its central contribution is a richer testing framework and practical selection guidance, rather than a claim that one estimator is best for every kind of dependence.
neurips-2023-beyond-normal-on-the-evalua.tldr: A diverse benchmark with known mutual information supports more informative evaluation and selection of classical and neural estimators.

paragraphs: Scientists often collect observations and experiments across environments, such as different laboratories or species. Learning causal structure from this evidence requires accounting for both interventions and differences between domains. This paper develops an approach that also allows latent confounders: unobserved factors that can influence multiple measured variables.

The authors first establish an equivalence between learning from observations across multiple domains and learning from interventions with unknown targets in a single domain. Combining observational and experimental evidence introduces further subtleties. To handle them, they derive causal invariances using do-calculus and formulate the S-Markov property, which connects distributions across domains to graphical criteria in a selection diagram.

This property supports S-FCI, a constraint-based algorithm that learns causal structure from observational and interventional data collected in different domains. The authors prove the algorithm is sound and encompasses existing constraint-based discovery algorithms. The result supplies a unified way to use heterogeneous causal evidence while accommodating hidden confounding; soundness supports the validity of its conclusions without asserting that every dataset uniquely determines the entire causal diagram.
neurips-2023-causal-discovery-from-obser.tldr: S-FCI uses a new causal invariance property to soundly combine observational and experimental evidence across domains with latent confounders.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning builds representations without supervised labels, but changes to graph connections or node attributes can undermine those representations. Earlier robustness approaches relied on empirical improvements. This paper investigates certification: establishing a formal basis for assessing robustness alongside measuring how a model performs in experiments.

The authors first introduce a unified criterion for evaluating and certifying graph contrastive learning robustness. They then propose Randomized Edgedrop Smoothing, or RES, as a technique for providing certifiable robustness to any graph contrastive learning model. The framework also establishes that its certified robustness can be preserved in downstream tasks, connecting representation-level guarantees to later uses of those representations.

An additional training method is designed to improve robust graph contrastive learning. Experiments on real-world datasets support the effectiveness of the approach for certification and robustness enhancement. The contribution therefore spans a criterion, a smoothing procedure, and a training method. Its significance lies in giving formal robustness support to a learning setting previously addressed empirically, without treating certification as an unrestricted guarantee against every possible attack.
neurips-2023-certifiably-robust-graph-co.tldr: Randomized Edgedrop Smoothing provides graph contrastive learning with robustness certificates that can carry through to downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Active domain adaptation chooses a small set of examples from a target domain for annotation. That choice depends partly on knowing where predictions are uncertain. The paper addresses approaches that emphasize target representativeness while obtaining uncertainty from an uncalibrated deterministic model, replacing a single estimate with a probabilistic treatment of representations and predictions.

The method uses variational inference to approximate their joint posterior distribution. Labeled examples are handled through a variational autoencoder and latent diffusion classifier, while unlabeled examples enter through knowledge distillation. Adversarial learning encourages a domain-invariant latent space. Sampling from the diffusion classifier then provides a predictive distribution for each example.

To select examples for labeling, the authors apply a t-test-based criterion to these samples. Its p-value captures both variation in predictions and ambiguity between categories. Experiments in standard and source-free active domain adaptation show better calibration than earlier methods and favorable performance on three datasets. The findings support using richer uncertainty estimates to guide annotation decisions when adapting across domains.
neurips-2023-diffusion-based-probabilist.tldr: A diffusion-based probabilistic classifier improves uncertainty calibration and guides target-sample annotation for active domain adaptation.

paragraphs: Adversarial contrastive learning uses adversarial data to learn representations that resist attacks and common corruptions without expensive annotations. A related technique, standard invariant regularization, encourages ordinary contrastive representations to ignore nuisance style factors. This paper investigates how independence from style can also help representations learned through adversarial contrastive training.

The authors use causal reasoning to interpret the learning process and introduce adversarial invariant regularization, or AIR. Their method combines AIR with standard invariant regularization. The theoretical result concerns distances in representation space: AIR implicitly encourages the distances between views of natural examples and their adversarial variants to be independent of style factors.

This matters because style-related variation can affect the relationships that contrastive learning uses to organize representations. The proposed regularization targets that dependence while retaining adversarial training. In experiments, adding invariant regularization significantly improves leading adversarial contrastive methods on both ordinary generalization and robustness in downstream tasks. The theoretical claim is an encouragement toward style-independent distances, while the reported performance gains are empirical.
neurips-2023-enhancing-adversarial-contr.tldr: Adversarial invariant regularization encourages style-independent representation distances and empirically improves downstream generalization and robustness.

paragraphs: Evaluating generated language requires ways to compare machine output with human writing. This paper approaches that comparison through patterns in estimated cross-entropy, drawing inspiration from psycholinguistic findings about periodicity in language entropy. The question is whether the way informational patterns vary can help reveal differences between generated and human-written text.

The authors introduce FACE, a family of metrics that applies Fourier analysis to estimated cross-entropy. Fourier analysis examines recurring variation in a signal, so this approach makes periodic structure part of the language comparison. FACE therefore provides a way to assess similarity through the pattern of estimated cross-entropy across text.

Using an open-ended generation task and experimental data from earlier studies, the authors find that FACE detects a gap between human and model language. The metrics also vary with model size, reflect different decoding sampling methods, and correlate well with other evaluation measures and human judgments. These findings support FACE as an empirical evaluation tool for the studied settings, with several connections to established indicators of generation quality.
neurips-2023-face-evaluating-natural-lan.tldr: FACE compares generated and human language through Fourier analysis of cross-entropy patterns, with empirical agreement with human judgments and other metrics.

paragraphs: A bandit learner must choose among options with uncertain rewards. This paper combines two goals: identifying and committing to the best option quickly, and collecting high rewards throughout a horizon of T rounds. It introduces Regret Optimal Best Arm Identification to study these goals together, rather than treating exploration speed and cumulative reward as separate objectives.

The proposed EOCP algorithm and its variants achieve asymptotically optimal regret for Gaussian and general bandits. Their commitment times scale as O(log T) with predetermined stopping and O(log² T) with adaptive stopping. Lower bounds establish that the predetermined version uses an optimal number of samples, while the adaptive versions are almost sample optimal.

Numerical results support the analysis and reveal an over-exploration effect in classic UCB algorithms. EOCP achieves smaller regret despite ending exploration much earlier: O(log T) rather than O(T) in the reported comparison. This suggests that prolonged exploration can be unnecessary and potentially harmful in this setting. The optimal-regret claim is asymptotic, and the sample-efficiency conclusion differs between predetermined and adaptive stopping.
neurips-2023-fast-and-regret-optimal-bes.tldr: EOCP combines fast commitment to the best arm with asymptotically optimal regret and optimal or nearly optimal sample complexity.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference uses simulated data to infer which underlying parameters could explain observations. Neural posterior estimation with discrete normalizing flows is an established approach, but scaling these models to high-dimensional problems can be difficult. This paper introduces flow matching posterior estimation, or FMPE, using continuous normalizing flows.

The approach draws on advances in generative modeling to allow more flexible architectures. Like diffusion models, flow matching avoids the architectural restrictions associated with discrete flows. The authors emphasize the combination of exact density evaluation, fast training, and compatibility with large architectures, which makes the approach attractive for complex scientific data.

FMPE performs competitively on an established simulation-based inference benchmark. In a more demanding gravitational-wave inference application, it outperforms comparable discrete-flow methods, reducing training time by 30% while substantially improving accuracy. This application provides evidence for improved scalability in a challenging scientific setting. The broader significance is the potential to expand neural posterior estimation to harder inference problems through a more flexible model family.
neurips-2023-flow-matching-for-scalable-.tldr: FMPE uses continuous flows for scalable posterior estimation, improving accuracy and cutting training time by 30% in gravitational-wave inference.

paragraphs: Designing a protein that binds a particular ligand requires shaping its binding pocket and choosing the residues that form it. FAIR addresses these decisions together, generating both pocket sequence and three-dimensional structure. It targets shortcomings of earlier methods in generation efficiency, ligand context, and the ability to include sidechain atoms.

FAIR follows a coarse-to-fine process. The first stage updates residue types and backbone coordinates using a hierarchical context encoder and modules for interactions between residues and between the pocket and ligand. The second stage includes sidechains and revises residue types to make sequence and structure consistent. Each refinement round updates all residues and structures together, while the ligand structure also changes to account for flexibility.

Evaluations show that FAIR designs high-quality pocket sequences and structures more efficiently than the compared baselines. The authors report average improvements exceeding 10% on AAR and RMSD. These results support joint, full-atom refinement as a useful design approach: the pocket’s components and flexible ligand are considered together throughout generation.
neurips-2023-full-atom-protein-pocket-de.tldr: FAIR jointly refines protein pocket sequences, full-atom structures, and flexible ligands, improving design quality and efficiency over baselines.

paragraphs: Emotion recognition can combine language, visual information, and sound because these sources provide complementary evidence. Missing one or more modalities weakens that combined understanding. This paper introduces IMDer, a method that recovers missing modalities to improve emotion recognition when the available inputs are incomplete.

IMDer uses a score-based diffusion model to transform Gaussian noise into data following the distribution of a missing modality. The available modalities condition the recovery process, helping guide and refine what is generated. This conditioning addresses semantic ambiguity: recovered information should fit the observed inputs as well as resemble the missing modality’s distribution.

The approach aims to satisfy distribution consistency and semantic alignment simultaneously. Feature visualizations support both properties, showing modality-specific distributions and alignment in meaning. Quantitative experiments report state-of-the-art emotion recognition accuracy across various patterns of missing modalities. The findings support conditional diffusion as a way to restore useful complementary information for recognition, with the observed inputs playing an active role in determining the recovered content.
neurips-2023-incomplete-multimodality-di.tldr: IMDer conditions diffusion-based recovery on available modalities to improve emotion recognition when language, visual, or acoustic inputs are missing.

paragraphs: Long-convolution sequence models offer an alternative to attention, but generating tokens one at a time can still be expensive. A naive implementation repeatedly processes the input sequence or stores its activations. This paper seeks to turn pretrained long convolutions into compact recurrences with constant computation and memory per generated token.

The method extracts a low-dimensional linear state-space model from each convolution layer, using rational interpolation and model-order reduction. This gives the layer a compact recurrent form for generation. The authors also modify convolution-based architectures such as Hyena by sharing filters across channels within heads, improving pretraining quality and reducing how many filters require distillation.

At 1.3 billion parameters, the resulting model achieves ten times the throughput of Transformers and 1.5 times that of Hyena, with no observed quality loss after distillation. These results connect an architectural change with a conversion procedure for faster generation. The throughput comparisons and quality preservation describe the reported model, while the broader method aims to make pretrained long-convolution architectures more efficient during autoregressive inference.
neurips-2023-laughing-hyena-distillery-e.tldr: Compact recurrent approximations of long convolutions enable faster generation, with reported throughput gains and no quality loss after distillation.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning a directed acyclic graph from data produced by a linear structural equation model. It views that model as a linear transformation of underlying random inputs, which the authors call root causes. The proposed setting assumes that only a few such causes are active, at least approximately, and also allows measurement noise.

The intuition is that a small number of generating events can affect many observed variables as their effects propagate through the graph. The authors develop an algorithm around this perspective and prove identifiability in the new setting. They also show that the true graph globally minimizes the L0 measure of the root-cause vector, which counts its nonzero entries.

This gives sparsity in the generating events a direct role in identifying graph structure. For data that satisfy the few-root-causes assumption, the authors report better performance than prior graph-learning methods. Both the theoretical motivation and the empirical comparison depend on this structured data-generation setting. The contribution is a way to exploit sparse initiating events even when their downstream effects spread broadly through the observed system.
neurips-2023-learning-dags-from-data-wit.tldr: Assuming few underlying generating events enables identifiable DAG learning and improved performance on data satisfying that assumption.

paragraphs: Online ad allocation requires assigning arriving impressions immediately while respecting advertisers’ budgets. Algorithms with ideal worst-case competitive ratios already exist for the studied problems, but their caution may leave useful predictability unexploited. This paper adds machine-learned predictions to algorithms for Display Ads and the generalized assignment problem.

The approach builds on earlier online allocation methods and uses a new analysis to balance two objectives. It should benefit when predictions are good while retaining robustness when predictions are poor. That balance matters because immediate decisions cannot wait for the full sequence of arrivals, and the usefulness of advance predictions can vary.

The authors evaluate their algorithm on synthetic and real-world data using a broad range of predictions. Across the reported experiments, it consistently outperforms the worst-case algorithm without predictions. The theoretical contribution concerns exploiting accurate predictions without abandoning protection against inaccurate ones. The empirical result shows that incorporating predictions improved allocation in the tested settings, rather than establishing that every prediction must improve every possible arrival sequence.
neurips-2023-online-ad-allocation-with-p.tldr: A prediction-augmented online allocation algorithm benefits from accurate forecasts while remaining robust to poor ones.

paragraphs: Smoothed online convex optimization involves making sequential decisions while paying costs for changing them. This paper considers a general setting where switching costs depend on multiple steps and feedback arrives late. It asks how machine-learning predictions can improve typical performance while preserving a dependable guarantee when those predictions are unreliable.

Robustness-Constrained Learning, or RCL, combines an untrusted prediction with a trusted expert online algorithm. A constrained projection adjusts the prediction to enforce robustness. For any positive lambda, the authors prove a competitive factor of 1 + lambda relative to the chosen expert. The guarantee is therefore explicitly tied to an expert reference rather than an unrestricted claim of optimality.

RCL also trains the prediction model with awareness of the later robustness adjustment, aiming to improve average-case performance after projection. The authors identify their result as the first provably robust learning-augmented approach covering both multi-step switching costs and delayed feedback. A battery-management case study demonstrates improvements in robustness and average performance, illustrating how the formal protection and learned predictions can work together.
neurips-2023-robust-learning-for-smoothe.tldr: RCL adjusts learned predictions to guarantee performance relative to an expert while addressing delayed feedback and multi-step switching costs.

paragraphs: A shared model can serve multiple tasks or domains, improving efficiency and potentially allowing knowledge transfer. Training becomes difficult when those tasks or domains impose different demands. This paper examines scalarization, which combines their losses into one objective, with particular attention to how the weighting of those losses affects training.

The motivation comes from earlier findings that simply averaging task losses can match more expensive state-of-the-art optimization methods. That observation raises questions about which aspects of joint training actually need more sophisticated treatment. The authors conduct a large-scale, unified analysis spanning both multi-task and multi-domain learning, varied task and domain combinations, and different model sizes.

Building on that analysis, they propose population-based training to search efficiently for scalarization weights when many tasks or domains are involved. The approach makes the relative importance of each loss a central optimization choice. The paper’s stated contribution is the broad analysis and resulting weight-search proposal; the abstract does not claim a universal advantage for a particular set of weights or a single training method.
neurips-2023-scalarization-for-multi-tas.tldr: A large-scale study of joint training motivates population-based search for loss weights across many tasks or domains.

paragraphs: Pretrained generative models can produce content associated with concepts that users want them to forget. Motivated by concerns about harmful, misleading, and inappropriate generation, this paper develops Selective Amnesia. The method draws inspiration from continual learning to make forgetting a deliberate intervention in an already trained model.

A central feature is controllability: users can specify how a concept should be forgotten. The method applies to conditional variational likelihood models, a family encompassing variational autoencoders and large text-to-image diffusion models. This scope connects the forgetting procedure to multiple generative frameworks rather than restricting the idea to one model type.

Experiments demonstrate induced forgetting across different models and kinds of concepts. These include entire classes in standard datasets and celebrity or nudity prompts in text-to-image systems. The findings show that the approach can target concepts at different levels of specificity. Its contribution is a controllable technique with demonstrations across model families; the reported forgetting results do not establish universal prevention of every possible unwanted generation.
neurips-2023-selective-amnesia-a-continu.tldr: Selective Amnesia uses a continual-learning-inspired procedure to induce user-controlled concept forgetting in pretrained generative models.

paragraphs: One hypothesis about working memory is that recurrent neural networks preserve continuous quantities through continuous families of stable activity states. A single network may need several such families for different contexts. Interference between them can roughen the network’s energy landscape, causing activity to drift toward isolated stable states and degrading the stored value.

This paper shows that adjusting synaptic weights can substantially reduce that interference. The authors define a loss measuring the roughness of the energy landscape along each embedded attractor manifold. Minimizing this loss directly targets the irregularities associated with drift, rather than treating interference as an unavoidable consequence of storing multiple continuous representations.

The reported result is a dramatic improvement in state stability without sacrificing capacity. This matters for models that need to maintain different continuous memories within the same recurrent network. The contribution demonstrates that suitable weight adjustment can attenuate detrimental interference; it does not require claiming that all interference disappears. The biological framing remains a hypothesis about how continuous working-memory representations may be sustained.
neurips-2023-simultaneous-embedding-of-m.tldr: Optimizing synaptic weights to smooth attractor landscapes can greatly improve continuous-memory stability without reducing network capacity.

paragraphs: A single photograph containing several identical objects can provide different views of the same underlying shape. Structure from Duplicates uses this observation to reconstruct object geometry, material, and illumination. Its key assumption is that the visible instances share geometry and material, allowing evidence from separate objects to constrain one reconstruction.

The framework first identifies the repeated instances and jointly estimates their positions and orientations in three dimensions. It introduces a Structure from Motion formulation designed to handle in-plane rotations robustly. An inverse graphics pipeline then jointly estimates the shared shape, shared material, and environmental lighting while maintaining consistency across the instances.

The authors report more realistic and detailed reconstructions than existing single-image models and multi-view approaches using a similar or larger number of observations. The result highlights the value of repetition as a source of multi-view information within one image. By treating duplicates as linked observations of a common object, the method extracts geometric evidence that would be missed if each visible instance were considered separately.
neurips-2023-structure-from-duplicates-n.tldr: Structure from Duplicates reconstructs shared object geometry, material, and lighting from repeated objects visible in a single image.

paragraphs: Preconditioning transforms a linear system into a form that is easier to solve. This paper develops a framework for finding approximately optimal preconditioners by exploiting matrix structure. Its technical foundation is a new class of semidefinite optimization problems, called matrix-dictionary approximation SDPs, together with an associated matrix-dictionary recovery problem.

For a positive definite matrix, the framework computes an epsilon-optimal diagonal preconditioner. Its runtime depends on the number of nonzero matrix entries and polynomial factors in the best achievable condition number and inverse accuracy, with logarithmic factors suppressed. This replaces the cited general-purpose semidefinite-programming runtime of at least order d^3.5 with a structure-sensitive bound.

The paper also gives a nearly quadratic-time solver for matrices that are graph Laplacian pseudoinverses or constant spectral approximations of them. This improves on the cited matrix-multiplication-based runtime for that structured setting. Together, the results show how specialized semidefinite optimization can improve both preconditioner construction and linear-system solving. The guarantees retain explicit conditions on matrix structure and, for diagonal preconditioning, conditioning and requested accuracy.
neurips-2023-structured-semidefinite-pro.tldr: Specialized semidefinite programs yield faster approximate diagonal preconditioning and nearly quadratic solvers for particular Laplacian-related systems.

paragraphs: Audio-visual segmentation identifies the image pixels belonging to sound-producing objects in a video. Training such a system with accurate pixel masks requires expensive annotation, and those masks are not always available. This paper studies learning the task from instance-level annotations, reducing the detail required in supervision while retaining pixel-level predictions as the goal.

The proposed WS-AVS framework learns alignment between audio and visual information at multiple scales. It uses multi-scale multiple-instance contrastive learning to build those correspondences under weaker supervision. The alignment is central because the system needs to connect what is heard with the visible regions responsible for the sound.

Experiments on AVSBench demonstrate the framework’s effectiveness in both single-source and multiple-source scenarios. These settings test segmentation when a video contains one sound source and when several sources must be handled. The contribution is a framework for learning detailed audio-visual localization from coarser annotations, supported by benchmark results. The reported findings establish effectiveness under weak supervision without claiming equivalence to every fully supervised approach.
neurips-2023-weakly-supervised-audio-vis.tldr: WS-AVS learns to segment sound-producing objects using instance-level annotations and multi-scale audio-visual contrastive alignment.
